eng507-collection-of-assessmnets-by-maha:
1. This course focuses on the linguistic study of speech sounds in a phonetic and
   phonological perspective. (true)
2. RP stands for (Received Pronunciation)
3. The suprasegmental features of a language relate to, “What you say?” (False)
4. Human sounds are divided into ________ broad categories. (two)
5. A speech sound in which air is at least partly blocked is called           .
   (consonant)
6. The phonology component examines the internal structure of word forms.
   (True)
7. At the end of this course, student will be able to understand the segmental and
   suprasegmental feature of the connected speech. (True)
8. Transcription will not be important part of the evaluation. (False)
9. Phonetics and phonology is the branch of linguistics which deals with the
   speech sounds. (human)
10.      GDB stands for ________ . (Graded Discussion Board)
11.      At the end of the course, the students will only be able to transcribe any
   kind of English text. (False)
12.      In this subject, we’ll study the sets of phonemes and sound patterns
   within a human language. (True)
13.      In British English (BBC accent), we have ________ sounds. (44)
14.      Phonologist describe the              consonants and vowels in a sound
   system (language). (contrastive)
15.      Diphthong is a vowel sound in which the tongue changes position to
   produce the sound of _______ vowels. (TWO)
16.      English diphthongs are divided into two categories. (true)
17.      IPA stands for ________. (International Phonetic Alphabet)

18.        English sounds have 9 Plosive sound. (false)
19.     A speech sound produced by completely or partly stopping the air being
  breathed out through the mouth is called ________. (consonant)
20.        Long vowels produce a ________ vowel sound. (long)
21.    Phonetic transcription is the ________ representation of speech sounds
  by means of symbols. (visual)
22.     In phonology, it matters whether sounds are ___________ or not, that
  is, whether substituting one sound for another gives a different meaning.
  (contrastive)
23.    Phonetics include the understanding of how sounds are                using
  mouth, nose, teeth and tongue. (articulated)
24.     There are three major types of phonetics: articulatory phonetics,
  acoustics phonetics and____________ phonetics. (auditory)
25.        The IPA is also maintaining a vibrant (website)
26.     Phonetics has been derived from the Greek word ‘phonetic’ meaning
  sound or voice. (False)
27.    Phonetics deals with production, transmission and ___________ of all
  human speech sounds. (reception)
28.     Phonetics as a field of study has a long history, going back certainly to
  well over __________ years ago. (two thousand)
29.     When soft palate is lowered and there is an obstruction in the mouth,
  we say that there is a nasal consonant. (true)
30.      In which branch of phonetics, we study the principal articulators and
  other processes related to speech production? (Articulatory)
31.        In most speech, soft palate is raised so that there is a velic closure.
  (true)
32.      A graph of a sound wave is very similar to a graph of the movements
  of the eardrum. (true)
33.     In the auditory field we do ________ tests to discover how the listener’s
  ear and brain interpret the information in the speech signal. (perceptual)

34.     Like other areas of grammar, a major change in the theory of phonology
  came about in ________. (1960s)
35.     Articulatory phonetics is the branch of phonetics which studies the way
  in which speech sounds are made (‘articulated’) by the vocal organs. (True)
36.     Acoustic phonetics is primarily dependent on the use of instrumental
  techniques of investigation such as _____________ software. (Praat)
37.      What did Peter Ladefoged explore about the areas of experimental
  phonetics in 1967? (The nature of vowel quality, Stress in respiratory
  activity, Perception and production of speech, All of the given options)
38.     The area of phonology is mainly related to specific ____________ rules
  within languages. (phonological)
39.    Most of the movements relevant to speech take place in the mouth and
  ________ area. (throat)
40.     The phonation process is the name given to the actions of
  the__________. (vocal folds)
41.    In most speech, soft palate is raised so that there is a velic closure.
  (True)
42.     Sibilant fricatives are weak and less audible and strident fricatives are
  strong and clearly audible. (False)
43.     The quality and intensity of fricative sounds varies greatly, but all are
  acoustically composed of energy at relatively high frequency. (True)
44.     BBC English has _______ approximant sounds. (four)
45.     The sound which is produced with back of the tongue and the soft palate
  (such as /k/ and /g/) is called ________. (velar)
46.      Consonantal sounds are divided, in terms of their manner of
  articulation, into two major types: obstruent and sonorants. (true)
47.     There are several basic ways to pronounce a consonant sound based on
  the configuration and __________ of the articulators involved. (interaction)
48.     The term ‘fricative’ is used in the phonetic classification of consonant
  sounds on the basis of their manner of articulation. (False)
49.      Plosion is the term used to refer to the ________ movement of air upon
  release. (outwards)

50.      Approximant is a phonetic term used to denote a _______ which makes
  very little obstruction to the airflow. (consonant)
51.     Trill is up and down movement of the top of the tip of tongue. (False)
52.     Which of the following is an example of affricate sound at the
  beginning and end of the English word church? (tʃ)
53.    A contrast of length (between short and long) is also sometimes
  encountered with_________. (vowels)
54.     In the articulation of vowels, the articulators do not come ______
  together and the air stream is relatively undisturbed. (close)
55.     In case of a stop sound, the closure and the burst are also ______ to
  judge. (easy)

making this sound a voiced alveolar lateral approximant. It may be compared with the sound [ɹ] in red

symbol for the voiced sound. There are no special symbols for voiceless nasals and it is written
as /m/-a combination of the letter for the voiced bilabial nasal and a diacritic indicating

What are Three dimensions of syllables?
The three dimensions of syllables are:

1. Onset: The consonant sound or cluster that begins the syllable.

2. Nucleus (or Peak): The vowel sound that forms the core or center of the syllable.

3. Coda: The consonant sound or cluster that ends the syllable.

What are Three plosive sounds?
The three plosive (or stop) sounds in English are:

1. /p/ (voiceless bilabial plosive)

2. /t/ (voiceless alveolar plosive)

3. /k/ (voiceless velar plosive)

What is Source-filter mechanism?

The source-filter mechanism is a model of speech production that explains how sounds are
generated in the human vocal tract. It consists of two main components:

1. Source: The vocal cords (or glottis) produce a sound source, such as a buzz or a vibration,
through vocal cord vibration.

2. Filter: The vocal tract, including the mouth and nose, acts as a filter that modifies the sound
source, shaping its frequency characteristics and producing the desired speech sounds.

This mechanism allows for the production of a wide range of speech sounds, from vowels to
consonants.

Voiced and voiceless sounds?
Voiced and voiceless sounds are classified based on the presence or absence of vocal cord
vibration:

Voiced Sounds

1. Produced with vocal cord vibration

2. Vocal cords are close together and vibrate

3. Examples: /b/, /d/, /g/, /z/, /v/

Voiceless Sounds

1. Produced without vocal cord vibration

2. Vocal cords are apart and do not vibrate

3. Examples: /p/, /t/, /k/, /s/, /f/

Praat software?
Praat is a free, open-source software for speech analysis, created by Paul Boersma and David
Weenink. It's widely used in phonetics, linguistics, and speech therapy.

Praat allows users to:

1. Record and edit speech sounds

2. Visualize and analyze acoustic properties (e.g., pitch, intensity, spectrograms)

3. Measure and annotate speech segments

4. Perform statistical analyses

Praat is available for Windows, macOS, and Linux.

Types of phonations?
There are mainly four possible glottis/larynx settings or types of phonations:

   ❖ Voiceless – when the folds are open apart and the air passing through the glottis freely (/t/
     or /p/).

   ❖ Voiced – when the folds are tight together and there is vibration during the air passage
     though the glottis (e.g., /b/ or /d/).

   ❖ Creaky voice – when there is a slight opening in the front and the arytenoid cartilages are
     tight together, so that the vocal folds can vibrate only at the anterior end (the small
     opening at the top).

   ❖ Breathy or murmuring sound – when the vocal folds are apart but still, they are
     vibrating - a breathy voice is like a whisper except voice.

Three types of sounds related to approximants?
The three types of sounds related to approximants are:

1. Liquids: /l/ and /r/ sounds, which are made by allowing air to flow freely through the mouth.

2. Glides: /j/ and /w/ sounds, which are made by moving the tongue or lips towards a specific
position.

3. Semivowels: Sounds that are intermediate between vowels and consonants, such as /j/ and /w/.

what is the function of first formant in the vowels?
The first formant (F1) is a critical acoustic cue for vowel identification, providing information
about vowel height, backness, and phonological contrasts.

what are the three sounds in the umbrella approximant?
The umbrella approximant, also known as the "w" sound, is actually a combination of three
distinct sounds:

1. Bilabial Approximant: /w/ (as in "wet")

2. Labiovelar Approximant: /ʊ̯/ (a blend of lip rounding and velarization)

3. Velar Approximant: /ɰ/ (a soft, velar sound)

Together, these three sounds blend to form the characteristic "w" sound in many languages.

Q. spectrogram help to know about bilabial sound.....2 [The most favourite of VU; V.V.IMP
for 2 marks questions. They are asking about stops or bilabial or approximants.]
      Voiced - vertical striations corresponding to the vibrations of the vocal folds
      Bilabial - locus of both second and third formants comparatively low
      Alveolar - locus of second formant about 1700–1800 Hz.
      Velar - usually high locus of the second formant
      Retroflex - general lowering of the third and fourth formants
      Stop - gap in pattern (with burst for voiceless and sharp formant beginning for voiced
       stops)
      Fricative - random noise pattern in higher frequency regions
      Nasal - formant structure similar to that of vowels (with formants at 250, 2500, and 3250)
      Lateral - formant structure similar to that of vowels (with formants at 250, 1200, and 2400)
      Approximant - formant structure similar to that in vowels, usually changing
Q. Memory for Speech [Another favourite of VU; V.V.IMP for 2 marks questions. They ask it
for speaking style, sound change or any one of them.]
The role of the memory for speech under the exemplar theory suggests that many instances of each
word are stored in memory and their phonetic variability is memorized rather than computed. The
main postulates of the concepts are given here:
    Language universal features: Broad phonetic classes (e.g., aspirated vs. unaspirated)
     derive from physiological constraints on speaking or hearing, but their detailed phonetic
     definitions are arbitrary—a matter of community norms.
    Speaking styles: No one style is basic (from which others are derived), because all are
     stored in memory. Bilingual speakers store two systems.
    Generalization and productivity: Exemplar theory says that generalization is also
     possible within productivity. Interestingly, productivity—the hallmark of linguistic
     knowledge in the phonetic implementation approach—is the least developed aspect of the
     exemplar theory.
    Sound change: Sound change is phonetically gradual and operates across the whole
     lexicon. It is a gradual shift as new instances keep on adding.
Q. Primary set of Cardinal Vowels
The primary set includes eight vowels in total (from 1 to 8); the front unrounded vowels [i, e, ε,
a], the back unrounded vowel [ɑ] and the rounded back vowels [ɔ, o, u].Symbol was given and we
had to write the lip jaw and tongue position.
Q. What specific terms are used for the consonants cluster Cc and ccc in syllable? (2)
Consonant sequences are called clusters (e.g., CC – two consonants or CCC – three consonants).
Most of the phonotactic analyses are based on the syllable structures and syllabic templates.

Q. Define syllable.
A unit of pronunciation having one vowel sound, with or without surrounding consonants, forming
the whole or a part of a word; e.g., there are two syllables in water and three in inferno.
Q. In what way Voice Onset time is related to the aspirated sounds? 2
In order to understand VOT, the three types of plosive sounds are to be explained – voiced,
voiceless and a voiceless aspirated sound. Most aspirated (largest positive VOT) at the top to most
voiced (largest negative VOT) at the bottom. The Navajo aspirated stops have a very large VOT
value that is quite exceptional (150 MS).

Zoom into a small piece of the waveform in the middle of the vowel and measure the period by
highlighting one complete cycle and noting the time associated with it (in the panel above the
waveform).

OR click Alt+backspace.

Languages of the world are; divided into two broad categories: stress timed language and syllable
timed languages.

The lowest three formants distinguish vowels from each other

Pakistani regional languages are the part of the rich linguistic regions. (Himalaya Hindu Kush
(HKH) region, one of the richest regions in the world linguistically and culturally) may be very
potential area for research in the fields of areal and typological linguistics (description of linguistic
features cross linguistically). While working on Pakistani regional languages, one may apply for
funding from international organizations (e.g., organization for endangered languages and
UNISCO).

ENG507_Glossary

1. Advanced tongue root (ATR) :Having the root of the tongue pulled forward so
   as to widen the pharynx (and, often, to raise the body of the tongue nearer to the
   roof of the mouth). Pharyngeal sounds are [-ATR], as the pharynx is narrowed.
2. affricate :A stop followed by a homorganic fricative.
3. allophone :A variant of a phoneme. The allophones of a phoneme form a set of
   sounds that (1) do not change the meaning of a word, (2) are all very similar to
   one another, and (3) occur in phonetic contexts different from one another—for
   example, syllable initial as opposed to syllable final. The differences between
   allophones can be stated in terms of phonological rules.
4. alternations :Variations in words that can be described in terms of phonological
   rules; for example, the difference between [ aI ] and [ I ] in divine, divin(ity).
5. alveolar :An articulation involving the tip or blade of the tongue and the alveolar
   ridge, as in English [ d ] in die.
6. alveolar ridge :The part of the upper surface of the mouth immediately behind
   the front teeth.
7. alveolo-palatal :Post-alveolar consonant produced with significant raising of the
   front of the tongue toward the palate.
8. ambisyllabic :Belonging to two syllables. A consonant such as [ p ] in happy is
   sometimes said to be ambisyllabic.
9. apical :An articulation involving the tip of the tongue.
10. approximant :An articulation in which one articulator is close to another but
   without the tract being narrowed to such an extent that a turbulent airstream is
   produced. In many forms of English, / j, l, r, w / are approximants.
11. articulator :One of several parts of the vocal tract that can be used to form
   speech sounds.

By ASFAND YARR

                              ENG507_Glossary

12. aspiration :A period of voicelessness after the release of an articulation, as in
   English in pie [ pÓaI].
13. assimilation :The change of one sound into another making it more similar to
   a neighboring sound, as in the change of underlying [ n ] to [ m ] in input [ ·ImpÁt
   ] or of underlying [ z ] to [ Z ] in does she [ ·dØZSi ].
14. back vowel :Vowel in which the body of the tongue is in the back part of the
   oral cavity (mouth). The vowels [ u, o, O, A ] form a set of back reference vowels.
15. bilabial :An articulation involving both lips, as in English [ m ] in my.
16. binary feature :A feature (for example, Lateral) that can be used to classify
   sounds in terms of two possibilities.
17. breathy voice :Another name for murmur; a type of phonation in which the
   vocal folds are only slightly apart so that they vibrate while allowing a high rate
   of airflow through the glottis, as in Hindi [ bH ].
18. broad transcription :A transcription that does not show a great deal of
   phonetic d etail; often a simple phonemic transcription.
19. cardinal vowels :A set of reference vowels first defined by Daniel Jones. The
   vowels of any language can be described by stating their relationships to the
   cardinal vowels.
20. citation form :The form a word has when it is cited or pronounced in
   isolation.
21. click :A stop made with an ingressive v elaric airstream, such as Zulu [ = ].
22. closed syllable :A syllable with a consonant at the end, as the first syllables
   in English magpie, pantry, completion.
23. coarticulation :The overlapping of adjacent articulations.
24. coda :The consonants occurring after the vowel in a syllable.
By ASFAND YARR

                               ENG507_Glossary

25. contour tone :A tone in a language such as Chinese that must be specified as
   a gliding movement within the pitch range.
26. coronal :A term for sounds articulated with the tip or blade of the tongue
   raised toward the teeth or the alveolar ridge (or, sometimes, the hard palate), such
   as [ T, s, t ].
27. creaky voice :See laryngealization.  declination :Gradual intonational pitch
   fall over the course of an utterance.
28. dental :Refers to sounds made with the tongue touching the teeth.
29. diacritic :Small added mark that can be used to distinguish different values
   of a symbol. For example, the addition of [ º] distinguishes a velarized from a
   nonvelarized sound, as in [ l º ] as opposed to [ l ].
30. diphthong :A vowel in which there is a change in quality during a single
   syllable, as in English [ aI 8] in high.
31. dorsal :Describing a sound articulated with the back of the tongue.  dorsum
   :The back of the tongue.
32. downdrift :The tendency for the pitch to fall throughout an intonational
   phrase.
33. ease of articulation :A phonetic force that impacts linguistic sound systems
   so that patterns that are easier to produce are more likely than difficult patterns.
34. ejective :A stop made with an egressive glottalic airstream, such as Hausa [ k'
   ].
35. epenthesis :The insertion of one or more sounds in the middle of a word, such
   as the pronunciation of sense as [ s”nts ].

By ASFAND YARR

                               ENG507_Glossary

36. exemplar theory :The idea that phonetic categories are represented in the
   mind as a set of all of the examples of the category that the speaker has produced
   and/or heard.
37. feature :A phonetic property of a sound. Some features like Coronal are fairly
   general, while others like Laminal Dental are more specific.
38. filter :In acoustic phonetics, a filter is an acoustic tube that enhances some
   frequency components of a sound source while decreasing the amplitudes of

• EXPLAIN the features (Voicing, MoA and PoA) of English consonants.

     There are 24 consonants in the RP accent of English.
     These consonants are described in terms of (1) voicing, (2) manners and place
     ‘Stop’ is often used as if synonymous with plosive.
     However, some phoneticians use it to refer to the class of sounds in which there is complete
      closure specifically in the oral cavity. In this case, sounds such as m, n are also stops.
     More precisely, they are nasal stops. In English, there are nine stops (six oral and three nasal):

                 bilabial      Alveolar    velar

- Voiced              p            t           k

+Voiced               b           d            g

(nasal) +Voiced m                 n                ŋ

     Apart from the above stops, in some varieties of English, the glottal stop /ʔ/ is found as in
      beaten [ˈbɪʔn̩ ].
     English voiceless stops (p, t, k) are also aspirated in the beginning of the words such as [phaI,
      thaI, khaI].
     It refers to a sound made with two articulators coming so close to each other that the air
      moving between them produces audible friction (or frication).
     Remember that there is no complete closure between the articulators and there is a very simple
      stricture (or narrowing of the air passage).

ENG507 (Notes for {Grand Quiz})

                                                       Lesson-10

                                  THE CONSONANTS OF ENGLISH-I

    1.   There are 24 consonants in the RP accent of English.
    2.   These consonants are described in terms of (1) voicing, (2) manners and (3) places of articulation.

               bilabial    labiodentals     dental     alveolar Post-    Palate- palatal               velar       glottal
                                                                alveolar alveolar
Plosive        p      b                                t     d                                         k       g
Fricative                  f            v θ        ð   s      z          ʃ     ʒ                                   h
Affricate                                                                ʧ    ʤ
Nasal                 m                                      n                                                 ŋ
Lateral                                                      l
Frictionless          w                                            r                   j
continuant
    3.  Stop’ is often used as if synonymous with plosive.
    4.  In English, there are nine stops (six oral and three nasal)
    5.  Apart from the above stops, in some varieties of English, the glottal stop /ʔ/ is found as in beaten [ˈbɪʔn ]̩ .
    6.  English voiceless stops (p, t, k) are also aspirated in the beginning of the words such as [𝑝ℎ aI, 𝑡 ℎ aI, 𝑘 ℎ aI].
    7.  Fricatives refer to a sound made with two articulators coming so close to each other that the air moving
        between them produces audible friction (or frication).
    8. Remember that there is no complete closure between the articulators and there is a very simple stricture (or
        narrowing of the air passage).
    9. In BBC English, we have several fricatives (both voiced and voiceless), as in fin [f], van [v], thin [θ], this
        [ð], sin [s], zoo [z], ship [ʃ], measure [ʒ], hoop [h].
    10. Other fricatives may be heard in some forms of English (or in restricted contexts or speech styles, such as
        the palatal fricative [ç]),
    11. A voiceless velar fricative [x] in Urdu, Pashto and Sindhi, a voiceless pharyngeal fricative [ħ] in Arabic, a
        voiced bilabial fricative [β] in Spanish.
    12. Very common fricative sounds are /f, v, s, z, θ, ʃ, ð, h/ whereas [ʒ] is a less common fricative sound.
    13. English fricatives are also divided into two categories (this distinction is made on the basis of energy made
        in their production);
    14. fortis: /f, s, θ, ʃ, h/
    15. lenis: /v, z, ð, ʒ/.
    16. Stops and fricatives are together called ‘obstruents’ and they are similar in three ways:
    17. They influence vowel length (vowels are shorter before voiceless obstruents),
    18. voiceless obstruents at final position are longer than their voiced counterparts (e.g., race vs. rays),
    19. obstruents are voiced only if the adjacent segments are also voiced (e.g., dogs).
    20. An affricate sound is a type of consonant which is made of a plosive followed by a fricative with the same
        place of articulation (so, it is a mixture of two steps or gestures).
    21. For example, /tʃ/ (the voiceless affricate) has /t/ and /ʃ/ as a sound at the beginning and end of the English
        words church /tʃɜ:tʃ/.
    22. Remember that although it is very strange to call the combination of a plosive and a fricative a single sound
        (an affricate) (as it has been deliberated for quite some time) yet experts argue that an affricate is a single
        segment and accordingly it should be treated as a single unit.
    23. There are two affricates in English: /tʃ/ and /dʒ/ (the first of these is voiceless, the second voiced) sounds as
        at the beginning and end of the English words church and judge. Both of them are post alveolar sounds by
        their place of articulation.

          lowered).
      25. For nasal sounds, two articulatory actions are necessary; (1) the soft palate (or velum) must be lowered to
          allow air to escape through nose, and (2) a closure must be made in the oral tract (in order to prevent air
          from escaping through it).
      26. This closure may be created at any place in the oral cavity (such as at lips position, for bilabial /m/ sound;
          at alveolar, for /n/ or at soft palate (velum) for /ŋ/ sound.
      27. English has these three nasal sounds (m, n and ŋ) which are very commonly found. All of them are nasal
          stops and they are voiced sounds.
      28. The consonants which make very little obstruction to the airflow are called approximants.
      29. These have traditionally been divided into two main groups: semivowels (such as /w/ in ‘wet’ and /j/ in
          ‘yet’) which are very similar to close vowels ([u] and [i]) but are produced as a rapid glide; and liquid
          sounds which have an identifiable constriction of the airflow (but they do not obstruct sufficiently to
          produce fricative noise, compression or the diversion of airflow)
      30. this category includes lateral sound i.e., /l/ as in ‘lead’ and /r/ sound as in ‘read’.
      31. Approximant sounds; therefore, are not fricative and never contain interruptions to the flow of air.
      32. The BBC accent of English has four approximant sounds:
      33. Bilabial: /w/ as in whack
      34. Alveolar: /l/ and /r/ as in lack and rack
      35. Palatal: /j/ as in yak
      36. Sometimes, experts need to differentiate among various kinds of /r/ approximant (tap, flap and trill).

    15. lenis: /v, z, ð, ʒ/.
    16. Stops and fricatives are together called ‘obstruents’ and they are similar in three ways:
    17. They influence vowel length (vowels are shorter before voiceless obstruents),
    18. voiceless obstruents at final position are longer than their voiced counterparts (e.g., race vs. rays),
    19. obstruents are voiced only if the adjacent segments are also voiced (e.g., dogs).
    20. An affricate sound is a type of consonant which is made of a plosive followed by a fricative with the same
        place of articulation (so, it is a mixture of two steps or gestures).
    21. For example, /tʃ/ (the voiceless affricate) has /t/ and /ʃ/ as a sound at the beginning and end of the English
        words church /tʃɜ:tʃ/.
    22. Remember that although it is very strange to call the combination of a plosive and a fricative a single sound
        (an affricate) (as it has been deliberated for quite some time) yet experts argue that an affricate is a single
        segment and accordingly it should be treated as a single unit.
    23. There are two affricates in English: /tʃ/ and /dʒ/ (the first of these is voiceless, the second voiced) sounds as
        at the beginning and end of the English words church and judge. Both of them are post alveolar sounds by
        their place of articulation.

Maha Malik’s Compilation                                                                                           Page 1

                               ENG507 (Notes for {Grand Quiz})

      24. Nasals are the consonantal sounds in which the air escapes through the nose (the soft palate i.e., velum is
          lowered).
      25. For nasal sounds, two articulatory actions are necessary; (1) the soft palate (or velum) must be lowered to
          allow air to escape through nose, and (2) a closure must be made in the oral tract (in order to prevent air
          from escaping through it).
      26. This closure may be created at any place in the oral cavity (such as at lips position, for bilabial /m/ sound;
          at alveolar, for /n/ or at soft palate (velum) for /ŋ/ sound.
      27. English has these three nasal sounds (m, n and ŋ) which are very commonly found. All of them are nasal
          stops and they are voiced sounds.
      28. The consonants which make very little obstruction to the airflow are called approximants.
      29. These have traditionally been divided into two main groups: semivowels (such as /w/ in ‘wet’ and /j/ in
          ‘yet’) which are very similar to close vowels ([u] and [i]) but are produced as a rapid glide; and liquid
          sounds which have an identifiable constriction of the airflow (but they do not obstruct sufficiently to
          produce fricative noise, compression or the diversion of airflow)
      30. this category includes lateral sound i.e., /l/ as in ‘lead’ and /r/ sound as in ‘read’.
      31. Approximant sounds; therefore, are not fricative and never contain interruptions to the flow of air.
      32. The BBC accent of English has four approximant sounds:
      33. Bilabial: /w/ as in whack
      34. Alveolar: /l/ and /r/ as in lack and rack
      35. Palatal: /j/ as in yak
      36. Sometimes, experts need to differentiate among various kinds of /r/ approximant (tap, flap and trill).

ENG507
➡️ Why Studying Phonetics and Phonology?

Studying phonetics and phonology is essential for understanding language sound systems.
Phonetics examines sound production, while phonology explores sound patterns and distribution.
This knowledge enhances language teaching, language acquisition, and speech therapy.

➡️ Evaluation Criteria for the Course

Evaluation criteria for phonetics and phonology courses include understanding phonetic
transcription, identifying speech sounds, analyzing sound patterns, and applying phonological
rules.

➡️ Introduction to Vowels and Consonants

Vowels are sounds made without obstructing airflow, while consonants involve obstruction.
English vowels include monophthongs (pure vowels) and diphthongs (gliding vowels).
Consonants encompass stops, fricatives, nasals, and approximants.

➡️ Introduction to English Vowels

English vowels include /i/, /ɪ/, /e/, /ɛ/, /æ/, /ɑ/, /ɔ/, /ʊ/, /u/, /y/. Vowel length and quality vary.

➡️ Introduction to English Diphthongs

English diphthongs include /ɔɪ/, /aɪ/, /aʊ/, /ɪə/, /ʊə/. Diphthongs combine two vowel qualities.

➡️ Introduction to English Consonants

English consonants encompass stops (/p/, /t/, /k/), fricatives (/f/, /v/, /s/), nasals (/m/, /n/, /ŋ/), and
approximants (/w/, /j/, /h/).

➡️ IPA Transcription of English Sounds

The International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) transcribes English sounds using unique symbols.

➡️ Introduction to Phonology

Phonology studies sound patterns and distribution in language.

➡️ Introduction to Phonetics

Phonetics examines sound production, including articulation, acoustic properties, and auditory
perception.

➡️ Phonetics vs. Phonology

Phonetics focuses on sound production, while phonology explores sound patterns and distribution.

➡️ Introduction to Key Concepts in Phonetics and Phonology

Key concepts include phonemes (distinct sounds), allophones (variant sounds), and phonetic
transcription.

➡️ Types of Phonetic Studies

Phonetic studies include articulatory, acoustic, auditory, and experimental phonetics.

➡️ Articulatory Phonetics

Articulatory phonetics examines sound production, focusing on articulatory gestures and manners.

➡️ Acoustic Phonetics

Acoustic phonetics analyzes sound waves.

➡️ Auditory Phonetics

Auditory phonetics investigates sound perception.

➡️ Experimental Phonetics and Phonology

Experimental phonetics and phonology employ empirical methods to study sound production and
patterns.

➡️ Generative Phonology

Generative phonology proposes rules to generate phonological patterns.

➡️ Articulatory Phonetics: Speech Production

Speech production involves articulatory gestures, sound waves, and oro-nasal processes.

➡️ The Oro-Nasal Process

The oro-nasal process distinguishes oral and nasal sounds.

➡️ Articulatory Gestures

Articulatory gestures include stop, fricative, nasal, and approximant.

➡️ Manners of Articulation

Manners of articulation encompass stop, fricative, nasal, and approximant.

➡️ Stop: Oral and Nasal

Stops involve blocking airflow orally or nasally.

➡️ Fricative Approximants

Fricatives involve partial obstruction, while approximants involve minimal obstruction.

➡️ Additional Consonantal Gestures

Consonantal gestures include trills, taps, and flaps.

➡️ The Articulation of Vowel Sounds

Vowel articulation involves tongue position, lip shape, and jaw movements

➡️ Suprasegmentals

Suprasegmentals include stress, intonation, and rhythm.

➡️ Why Transcribe?

Transcription aids language teaching, language acquisition, and speech therapy.

➡️ PHONEMIC AND PHONETIC

Phonemic transcription represents distinct sounds, while phonetic transcription represents actual
sounds.

➡️ Broad and Narrow Transcription

Broad transcription focuses on phonemes, while narrow transcription includes allophones.

➡️ IPA Resource: The North Wind and The Sun Story

The North Wind and The Sun story is a classic IPA transcription exercise. It demonstrates phonetic
transcription using International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) symbols, helping learners develop
phonetic awareness and transcription skills.

➡️ IPA Story: Explanation

This story explains IPA transcription principles, such as representing sounds, not letters. It
highlights phonetic nuances like /θ/ (th) and /ŋ/ (ng), illustrating the importance of accurate
transcription.

➡️ IPA Story: Broad Transcription

Broad transcription focuses on phonemes (distinct sounds), using symbols like /p/, /t/, /k/. This
transcription type emphasizes linguistic contrasts.

➡️ IPA Story-Phonetic Transcription

Phonetic transcription represents actual sounds, including allophones (variant sounds). Symbols
like [pʰ], [t̚], [kʲ] capture phonetic details.

Transcription Beyond Words:

Transcription extends beyond words to capture connected speech phenomena.

Transcription Beyond Words: Word Stress

Word stress transcription indicates syllable emphasis, using symbols like /ˈ/ (primary stress) and
/ˌ/ (secondary stress).

Transcription Beyond Words: Accent

Accent transcription represents regional or social variations in pronunciation.

Transcription Beyond Words: Phrases

Phrase transcription captures sound changes across word boundaries.

➡️ The Consonants of English

English consonants include:

   -   Stop consonants (/p/, /t/, /k/)
   -   Fricatives (/f/, /v/, /s/)

   -   Affricates (/tʃ/, /dʒ/)
   -   Nasals (/m/, /n/, /ŋ/)
   -   Approximants (/w/, /j/, /h/)

Stop Consonants: Stop consonants involve blocking airflow orally or nasally.

   -   Fricatives: Fricatives involve partial obstruction.
   -   Affricates: Affricates combine stop and fricative characteristics.
   -   Nasals: Nasals involve airflow through the nasal cavity.
   -   Approximants: Approximants involve minimal obstruction

➡️ Aspects of Connected Speech

Connected speech involves:

   -   Co-articulation
   -   Assimilation
   -   Elision
   -   Junction

Q. Define the term 'rhotic accent'
A rhotic speaker pronounces the letter "R" in hard and water. In other words, rhotic speakers
pronounce "R" in all positions.
Q. Two types of sounds involving aspiration process - 2 marks
Phonetically, aspiration is the result of the vocal cords being widely parted at the time of the
articulatory release. Is some languages (such as English) aspiration is allophonic while in others
(such as Urdu) it is phonemic.
Q. Tone language's
In the case of tone languages, it is usual to identify tones as being a property of individual syllables,
whereas an intonational tone may be spread over many syllables. Similarly, in the analysis of
English intonation, tone refers to one of the pitch possibilities for the tonic (or nuclear) syllable, a
set usually including fall, rise, fall–rise and rise fall, though others are also suggested by various
experts.
Q. feel, father, put describe vowels with tongue position
A low vowel (such as a in “father” or “had”) is produced with the tongue relatively flat. You may
also be able to feel the [i] as somewhat further forward
Q. pronouncing /u/ tongue position is:
Vowel /ʊ/ is often pronounced with spread lips in this variety of English. It is like the back of the
tongue is raised for an /u/ vowel sound creating a secondary (articulation) constriction.
Q. H and L stand for in break indicates 2 marks
One of the most recently developed methods is called the ‘tone and break indices’ (ToBI). This
method is used for the description of intonation (H/L) representing pitch changes and showing
pitch accent – phrase accent and boundary by showing tone and break indices. This is based on
describing High (H) and Low (L) pitches in a sentence representing pitch changes and showing
pitch accent – phrase accent and boundary (of the phrase).
Q. Define relation of F1 and F2 in vowel sound?
Acoustically, vowels are mainly distinguished by the first two formant frequencies F1 and F2; F1
is inversely related to the vowel height (which means that smaller F1 amplitude = higher vowels),
and F2 is related to the front or back of the vowels (smaller F2 amplitude = more back vowels).
Q. What does Grey areas indicate in chart
Areas of darker gray represent impossible articulations.
Q. Define sibilant fricative
The fricatives [s, z, ʒ, ʃ] are called sibilant sounds. Sibilant fricatives (such as s, ʃ) are strong and
clearly audible and strident fricatives are weak and less audible (such as θ, f).

       Place of articulation = alveolar. The narrowing of the vocal tract involves the tongue tip
       &the alveolar ridge
       Manner of articulation = oral stop. (The narrowing is complete -- the tongue is completely
       blocking off airflow through the mouth. ...
       Voicing = voiced. articulation, phonation, etc.
Q. Stress Rules: (V.V.V. IMP)
2 types of stress are important. Firstly, stress on a syllable within a word (the lexical stress) which
changes the grammatical category of a word (compare insult with insult) and also change meaning
among other things. On the other hand, stress on a word or certain words in a phrase or sentence.
This type of stress (on word(s) within sentences) is called sentence level or prosodic stress. This
is, in fact, a change or modification to word level stress in a sentence which is basically a change
of ‘beat’ on certain words in a sentence. Remember that, we create ‘rhythm’ in spoken language
on the basis of stress.
Q. Homograph
It is a group (usually a pair) of words that are spelled the same way, & may or may not be
pronounced the same way, although the difference in pronunciation is often just a shift in the
accented syllable. There is a whole class of homographs that end in -ate, usually with one being a
verb and the other being a noun or an adjective related to it. E.g : "Advocate" can be pronounced
with a long "a" sound and mean "to speak or write in support of" "Advocate" can also be
pronounced with a short "a" sound and refer to a person who supports or pleads the cause of
another.
Q. Supra segmental
‘Supra’ means above (beyond) and ‘segments’ means sounds (such as vowels and consonants) so
the term ‘suprasegmental’ means ‘above sounds’. The term suprasegmental was initially invented
to refer to aspects of sound such as intonation that did not seem to be the properties of individual
segments (i.e. the vowels and consonants of which speech is composed).. There has never been
full agreement about how many suprasegmental features are to be found in speech, but pitch,
loudness, tempo, juncture, syllable, rhythm and stress are the most commonly mentioned ones.
Q. Phonation types:
               Voiceless – when the folds are open apart and the air passing through the glottis
               freely (/t/ or /p/).

Essential requirements of human speech production, any 3

There are three possible mechanisms involved in human speech production.

   1) The most common one is the moving of air by compression of the lungs so that
      the air is expelled through the vocal tract this is called a pulmonic airstream.

   2) The second one is the glottalic (produced by the larynx with closed vocal folds - it
      is moved up and down like the plunger of a bicycle pump).

   3) last one is called velaric (where the back of the tongue is pressed against the soft
      palate or velum

Airstream mechanism names

   ❖ Pulmonic Airstream Mechanism
   ❖ Glottalic Airstream Mechanism
   ❖ Velaric Airstream Mechanism

Define Rhotic accent

In rhotic (e.g., some American) accents, on the other hand, /r/ may occur before
consonants (as in ‘cart’ /ka:rt/) and before a pause (as in ‘car’ /kɑ:r/).

most speakers of American English speak with a rhotic accent, but there are non-rhotic
areas including the Boston area, lower-class New York and the Deep South.

Other names of narrow and broad transcription

Narrow and broad transcription in phonetics can also be referred to by the following
alternative terms:

Narrow Transcription:

   ❖ Phonetic Transcription
   ❖ Impressionistic transcription

Broad Transcription:

          ❖ Phonemic Transcription

Rules for English Consonant Allophones (ECA):

Based on the above discussion on overlapping and co-articulatory gestures, the rules for
English consonantal allophones are summarized here in this topic. Remember that it is
just a list of a set of formal statements simply describing the behavior of a language.
These are not the kind of prescriptive grammar rules that people are expected to abide
by.

   1) Consonants are longer when at the end of a phrase (e.g., bib, did, don and nod).

   2) Voiceless stops (e.g., p, t, k) are aspirated when they are syllable initial (pip, test,
      kick).

   3) Voiced obstruents (b, d, g, v, ð, z, ʒ) are voiced only when they occur at the end
      of an utterance or before a voiceless sound.

   4) 4. Voiced stops (b, d, g) and affricate (dʒ) are voiceless when they are syllable
      initial (except when immediately preceded by a voiced sound – compare a day with
      this day).

   5) Voiceless stops (p, t, k) are unaspirated after /s/ in words such as spew, stew and
      skew.

   6) Voiceless obstruent’s (p, t, k, tʃ, f, θ, s, ʃ) are longer than their voiced counterparts
      (b, d, g, dʒ, v, ð, z, ʒ) at the end of a syllable (e.g., cap - cab and back – bag).

   7) Approximants (w, r, j, l) are at least partially voiceless when they occur after initial
      voiceless stop sounds (e.g., play, twin, cue).

   8) The gestures for consecutive stops overlap, so that stops are unexploded when
      they occur before another stop (e.g., apt and rubbed).

   9) In many accents of English, syllable final voiceless stops /p, t, k/ are accompanied
      by an overlapping glottal stop gesture (e.g., tip, pit, kick).

   10) /t/ is replaced by a glottal stop when it occurs before an alveolar nasal (e.g.,
       beaten).

   11) Nasals are syllabic at the end of a word - after an obstruent (e.g., leaden, chasm).

   12) The lateral /l/ is syllabic at the end of a word - a consonant (e.g., paddle, whistle).

What are the methods for analyzing intonation:

There are several ways for analyzing intonation. In some approaches, the pitch patterns
are described as contours and are further analyzed in terms of levels of pitch as pitch
phonemes and morphemes. In others, the patterns are described as tone units or tone
groups, analyzed further as contrasts of nuclear tone, tonicity, etc. The three variables (1)
pitch range; (2) height and (3) direction are generally distinguished. Some approaches
(especially within pragmatics), operate with a much broader notion than that of the tone
unit (i.e., intonational phrasing is a structured hierarchy of the intonational constituents in
conversation). A formal category of intonational phrase is also sometimes recognized
(i.e., an utterance span dominated by boundary tones). One of the most recently
developed methods is called the ‘tone and break indices’ (ToBI). This method is used for
the description of intonation (H/L) representing pitch changes and showing pitch accent

– phrase accent and boundary by showing tone and break indices. This is based on
describing High (H) and Low (L) pitches in a sentence representing pitch changes and
showing pitch accent – phrase accent and boundary (of the phrase).

There are 44 sounds in English RP (BBC) accent. Out of them, 20 are vowels which, in turn, are
further divided into pure vowels and diphthongs. Pure vowels or monophthongs are 12 out of

Q. VOT:
Voice Onset Time (VOT) is a term used in phonetics referring to the point in time at which
vocalfold vibration starts in relation to the release of a closure (during the production of plosive
sounds). In order to understand VOT, the three types of plosive sounds are to be explained –
voiced, voiceless and a voiceless aspirated sound. For example, during the production of a fully
voiced plosive (e.g., /b/ or /g/), the vocal folds vibrate throughout; in a voiceless unaspirated
plosive (such as /p/ or /t/), there is a delay (or lag) before voicing starts; and, in a voiceless

                                                          um
aspirated plosive (e.g., /pʰ/ or /tʰ/), the delay is much longer, depending on the amount of
aspiration. The amount of this delay is called Voice Onset Time (VOT) which in relation to the
types of plosive varies from language to language.
Q. Articulators:

                                                nj
We can only produce speech sounds by moving parts of our articulators (body parts), and this is
done by the contraction of muscles. Most of the movements relevant to speech take place in the
mouth and throat area (though we should not forget the activity in the chest for breath control),
                                  lA
and parts of the mouth and throat area that we move when speaking. These are called
articulators. In this branch of phonetics, we study the principal articulators (such as tongue, lips,
lower jaw and the teeth, velum or soft palate, uvula and larynx) and other processes related to
speech production. This includes the features of various sounds such as vowels and consonants
and their specific properties including places and manners of articulation, phonation, etc.
                 e

Q. Lax vowels:
              de

Lax vowels, remember, are short. Lax sounds are produced with less muscular effort and
movement, and are relatively short and indistinct vowel sounds (e.g., i, e, ɒ, æ, ʌ, ʊ, ə vowels
articulated near the center of the vowel area) compared to tense sounds (e.g., u:, i:, ɜ:, a:, ʊə, iə).
In other words, a lax vowel is said to be the one produced with relatively little articulatory
      A

energy.
Q.Nasalization
Nasalization is an articulatory process whereby a sound is made ‘nasal’ (when the air is passing
through the nasal cavity) due its adjacent nasal sound (it is an articulatory influence of an
adjacent nasal consonant, as in words like mat or hand). A vowel can also be nasalised in words
like man (when /a/ may be articulated with the soft palate lowered throughout), because of the
nasal consonants’ influence (this is called anticipatory coarticulation).
Q. Lexical stress
Lexical stress is basically related to the primary stress applied at syllable level (when only one
syllable is stressed) that has the ability to change the meaning and the grammatical category of a
word as in the case of ‘IMport’ (noun) and ‘imPORT’ (verb).

There are 44 sounds in English RP (BBC) accent. Out of them, 20 are vowels which, in turn, are
further divided into pure vowels and diphthongs. Pure vowels or monophthongs are 12 out of
which 5 are long and 7 are short vowels.
Q. VOT:
Voice Onset Time (VOT) is a term used in phonetics referring to the point in time at which
vocalfold vibration starts in relation to the release of a closure (during the production of plosive
sounds). In order to understand VOT, the three types of plosive sounds are to be explained –
voiced, voiceless and a voiceless aspirated sound. For example, during the production of a fully
voiced plosive (e.g., /b/ or /g/), the vocal folds vibrate throughout; in a voiceless unaspirated
plosive (such as /p/ or /t/), there is a delay (or lag) before voicing starts; and, in a voiceless

                                                          um
aspirated plosive (e.g., /pʰ/ or /tʰ/), the delay is much longer, depending on the amount of
aspiration. The amount of this delay is called Voice Onset Time (VOT) which in relation to the
types of plosive varies from language to language.
Q. Articulators:

                                                nj
We can only produce speech sounds by moving parts of our articulators (body parts), and this is
done by the contraction of muscles. Most of the movements relevant to speech take place in the
mouth and throat area (though we should not forget the activity in the chest for breath control),
                                  lA
and parts of the mouth and throat area that we move when speaking. These are called
articulators. In this branch of phonetics, we study the principal articulators (such as tongue, lips,
lower jaw and the teeth, velum or soft palate, uvula and larynx) and other processes related to
speech production. This includes the features of various sounds such as vowels and consonants
and their specific properties including places and manners of articulation, phonation, etc.
                 e

Q. Lax vowels:
              de

Lax vowels, remember, are short. Lax sounds are produced with less muscular effort and
movement, and are relatively short and indistinct vowel sounds (e.g., i, e, ɒ, æ, ʌ, ʊ, ə vowels
articulated near the center of the vowel area) compared to tense sounds (e.g., u:, i:, ɜ:, a:, ʊə, iə).
In other words, a lax vowel is said to be the one produced with relatively little articulatory
      A

energy.
Q.Nasalization
Nasalization is an articulatory process whereby a sound is made ‘nasal’ (when the air is passing
through the nasal cavity) due its adjacent nasal sound (it is an articulatory influence of an
adjacent nasal consonant, as in words like mat or hand). A vowel can also be nasalised in words
like man (when /a/ may be articulated with the soft palate lowered throughout), because of the
nasal consonants’ influence (this is called anticipatory coarticulation).
Q. Lexical stress
Lexical stress is basically related to the primary stress applied at syllable level (when only one
syllable is stressed) that has the ability to change the meaning and the grammatical category of a
word as in the case of ‘IMport’ (noun) and ‘imPORT’ (verb).

is the glide from one vowel quality to another one (so basically it is a glide). The BBC accent of
English contains a large number (eight in total) of diphthongs including three ending at /ɪ/ (eɪ, aɪ,
ɔɪ – as in words bay, buy and boy), two ending at /υ/ (əʊ, aʊ – as in words no and now) English

Q. What are the aim and objective of the course Eng507?
            Aim and objective of course are:
                understand how human sound is produced;
                know the physical properties of human sounds;
                study the suprasegmental features and features of the connected speech;
                have a greater awareness of IPA symbols and transcribe any kind of English text;
                prepare themselves for more advanced level course in Experimental Phonology for their
                   detailed future research work;
                learn about the modern software used in phonological research.

Q. Differentiate vowel and consonant.
         Human sounds are divided into two broad categories: consonants and vowels. A consonant is a
 speech sound in which air is at least partly blocked whereas vowel is a sound in which there is no
 obstruction found and the air passes through the cavity freely.

Q. How we classify consonant?
            A consonant is classified in terms of the places of articulation, manners of articulation and
 voicing.

Q. How we classify vowel?
     Vowel is classified in terms of the position of tongue, the part of tongue and lip-rounding.

 between mouth and ear according to the principles of acoustics (the branch of physics devoted to the study
 of sound).

 as mediated by ear, auditory nerve and brain..

                             ENG507_Phonetics and Phonology
                            Quiz from Assessments (Final-Term)

                        A Special Thanks to OxyGen
   1. Laryngealized (creaky) sound /b̰/ exists in ________. (Hausa)
   2. In phonetics and phonology, speech sounds (segments), using basic units of contrast, are
      defined as gestures. (True)
   3. Gestures are treated as the abstract characterizations of articulatory events with an
      _________ time dimension. (intrinsic)
   4. Many languages (including English) have the labiodental fricatives [f, v]. (False)
   5. Ejective affricate /tsʼ/ is found in ________. (Navajo)
   6. A large number of non-English sounds are to be found in other languages (such as Iranian
      and African languages). (True)
   7. An articulatory target refers to the ________ target position of the articulators for the
      production of a specific speech sound. (hypothetical)
   8. Dental sounds are present only in the American English. (False)
   9. In English and most of other languages nasals are voiced. (True)
   10.As voiceless nasals are comparatively rare, they are symbolized simply by adding the
      voiceless diacritic [ ̥] above the symbol for the voiced sound. (False)
   11.The fricatives [s, z, ʒ, ʃ] are called ________ sounds. (sibilant)
   12.A better way of dividing fricatives is to separate them into groups on a purely ________
      basis. (auditory)
   13.It is a usual /r/ approximant or unusual rhotic approximate [ɹ] found in ________ English.
      (American)
   14.In all forms of English, the air flows freely without audible friction, making this sound a
      ________ alveolar lateral approximant. (voiced)
   15.Laterals are usually presumed to be _______ approximants unless a specific statement to
      the contrary is made. (voiced)
   16.A ‘laryngeal gesture’ would specify all supraglottal characteristics. (False)
   17.In the sections on various stop sounds in world languages, we studied _______ types of
      stop sounds. (13)
   18.An ‘oral gesture’ would specify characteristics of phonation. (False)
   19.Speech segments are modeled as sets of gestures that have their own _______ temporal
      structure allowing them to overlap one way or the other. (intrinsic)
   20.Acoustic phonetics is the study of the ________ properties of speech, and aims to analyze
      sound wave signals. (physical)
   21.Acoustic analysis describes the durational characteristics, articulatory properties and
      _________ differences through physiological measurement. (phonetic)
   22.In acoustics, it is possible to measure and analyze vibrations (physical properties) by
      mathematical techniques. (True)
   23.Source-filter theory is an important concept in auditory phonetics. (False)

                            Quiz from Assessments (Final-Term)

   24.Acoustics is mainly devoted to the principles of physics involving the latest technology
      such as computer software ________. (Praat)
   25.Sound travels from a noise-making source (i.e., the vocal fold vibration) to the_______.
      (lips)
   26.Acoustic analysis not only gives us the features of a sound but also tells us about the
      duration or length of a speech sound. (True)
   27.The experts of phonetics are particularly interested in analyzing ________ acoustically.
      (vowels)
   28.Acoustic Analysis of Vowels describes vowels in terms of numbers (in a language that how
      many vowels are possible). (True)
   29.In source-filter theory, the vocal folds (at ________) are then a source of sound energy.
      (larynx)
   30.According to Source-filter theory, source refers to the _________ of the vibrating larynx.
      (waveform)
   31.Acoustic phonetics particularly involves electronics and some grounding in physics.
      (True)
   32.The air in the vocal tract is set in vibration by the action of the vocal folds. (True)
   33.All voiced sounds are distinguishable from one another by their formant structure
      (frequencies). (True)
   34.Using computer programs, we can analyze vowel sounds by showing their components
      through the display (spectrogram). (True)
   35.The resonance frequency of the particular resonance mode _________ when a constriction
      is located at a node of that resonance mode. (decreases) (increases in system)
   36.In spectrograms: the frequency of the components is shown on the _________ scale.
      (vertical)
   37.The resonance frequencies change in a predictable way when the tube is _________at
      various locations. (squeezed)
   38.The vocal tract as a tube with a uniform diameter has simultaneous resonance
      frequencies—several different pitches at the same time. (True)
   39.The resonance frequency of the particular resonance mode _________ when a constriction
      is located at a node of that resonance mode. (squeezed)

Quiz from Assessments (Mid-Term)

                             ENG507_Phonetics and Phonology
                             Quiz from Assessments (Mid-Term)

1. This course focuses on the linguistic study of speech sounds in a phonetic and phonological
   perspective. (true)
2. RP stands for (Received Pronunciation)
3. The suprasegmental features of a language relate to, “What you say?” (False)
4. Human sounds are divided into ________ broad categories. (two)
5. A speech sound in which air is at least partly blocked is called . (consonant)
6. The phonology component examines the internal structure of word forms. (True)
7. At the end of this course, student will be able to understand the segmental and suprasegmental
   feature of the connected speech. (True)
8. Transcription will not be important part of the evaluation. (False)
9. Phonetics and phonology is the branch of linguistics which deals with the speech sounds.
   (human)
10.GDB stands for ________ . (Graded Discussion Board)
11.At the end of the course, the students will only be able to transcribe any kind of English text.
   (False)
12.In this subject, we’ll study the sets of phonemes and sound patterns within a human language.
   (True)
13.In British English (BBC accent), we have ________ sounds. (44)
14.Phonologist describe the consonants and vowels in a sound system (language). (contrastive)
15.Diphthong is a vowel sound in which the tongue changes position to produce the sound of
   _______ vowels. (TWO)
16.English diphthongs are divided into two categories. (true)
17.IPA stands for ________. (International Phonetic Alphabet)
18.English sounds have 9 Plosive sound. (false)
19.A speech sound produced by completely or partly stopping the air being breathed out through
   the mouth is called ________. (consonant)
20.Long vowels produce a ________ vowel sound. (long)
21.Phonetic transcription is the ________ representation of speech sounds by means of symbols.
   (visual)
22.In phonology, it matters whether sounds are ___________ or not, that is, whether substituting
   one sound for another gives a different meaning. (contrastive)
23.Phonetics include the understanding of how sounds are using mouth, nose, teeth and tongue.
   (articulated)
24.There are three major types of phonetics: articulatory phonetics, acoustics phonetics
   and____________ phonetics. (auditory)
25.The IPA is also maintaining a vibrant (website)
26.Phonetics has been derived from the Greek word ‘phonetic’ meaning sound or voice. (False)
27.Phonetics deals with production, transmission and ___________ of all human speech sounds.
   (reception)

Maha Malik’s Compilation

                              ENG507_Phonetics and Phonology
                              Quiz from Assessments (Mid-Term)

28.Phonetics as a field of study has a long history, going back certainly to well over __________
   years ago. (two thousand)
29.When soft palate is lowered and there is an obstruction in the mouth, we say that there is a
   nasal consonant. (true)
30.In which branch of phonetics, we study the principal articulators and other processes related to
   speech production? (Articulatory)
31.In most speech, soft palate is raised so that there is a velic closure. (true)
32.A graph of a sound wave is very similar to a graph of the movements of the eardrum. (true)
33.In the auditory field we do ________ tests to discover how the listener’s ear and brain interpret
   the information in the speech signal. (perceptual)
34.Like other areas of grammar, a major change in the theory of phonology came about in
   ________. (1960s)
35.Articulatory phonetics is the branch of phonetics which studies the way in which speech sounds
   are made (‘articulated’) by the vocal organs. (True)
36.Acoustic phonetics is primarily dependent on the use of instrumental techniques of
   investigation such as _____________ software. (Praat)
37.What did Peter Ladefoged explore about the areas of experimental phonetics in 1967? (The
   nature of vowel quality, Stress in respiratory activity, Perception and production of speech, All
   of the given options)
38.The area of phonology is mainly related to specific ____________ rules within languages.
   (phonological)
39.Most of the movements relevant to speech take place in the mouth and ________ area. (throat)
40.The phonation process is the name given to the actions of the__________. (vocal folds)
41.In most speech, soft palate is raised so that there is a velic closure. (True)
42.Sibilant fricatives are weak and less audible and strident fricatives are strong and clearly
   audible. (False)
43.The quality and intensity of fricative sounds varies greatly, but all are acoustically composed
   of energy at relatively high frequency. (True)
44.BBC English has _______ approximant sounds. (four)
45.The sound which is produced with back of the tongue and the soft palate (such as /k/ and /g/)
   is called ________. (velar)
46.Consonantal sounds are divided, in terms of their manner of articulation, into two major types:
   obstruent and sonorants. (true)

Why Studying Phonetics and Phonology?
   - Improved pronunciation: Knowing the correct production and sound of
      English vowels, diphthongs, and consonants helps learners achieve
      accurate pronunciation.
   - Enhanced language teaching: Teachers can better instruct students on
      English pronunciation and decoding skills.
   - Language learning: Understanding phonetics and phonology aids in
      learning English and other languages.
   - Speech therapy: Studying phonetics and phonology helps speech therapists
      diagnose and treat speech disorders.
   - Language development: Researchers can understand how children acquire
      language and how language changes over time.
   Focus Language – English: English is a widely spoken language with a
   complex sound system, making it an ideal focus for phonetics and phonology
   studies.
   Introduction to Vowels and Consonants
      - Vowels: Sounds made without blocking the airflow in the mouth (e.g.,
          /i/ in "bit").
      - Consonants: Sounds made by blocking the airflow (e.g., /p/ in "pat").
   Introduction to English Vowels
English has monophthong vowels (single, pure sounds) and diphthongs (gliding
sounds).
      - Monophthong vowels: /i/ (bit), /e/ (bet), /a/ (bat), /o/ (bot), /u/ (but)
      - Diphthongs: /ai/ (buy), /au/ (how), /oi/ (boy)
   Introduction to English Consonants
English consonants include stops, fricatives, nasals, liquids, and approximants.

     - Stops: /p/ (pat), /t/ (tot), /k/ (cat)
     - Fricatives: /s/ (sat), /z/ (zat), /f/ (fat)
     - Nasals: /m/ (mat), /n/ (nat), /ŋ/ (sing)
     - Liquids: /l/ (lat), /r/ (rat)
     - Approximants: /w/ (wat), /j/ (yes)
  IPA Transcription of English Sounds: The International Phonetic Alphabet
  (IPA) represents English sounds with unique symbols, ensuring accurate
  representation and transcription.
  Introduction to Phonology: Phonology studies the sound system of
  languages, examining sound distribution, patterns, and rules.
  Introduction to Phonetics: Phonetics examines the physical properties of
  speech sounds, including production, acoustic properties, and perception.
  Phonetics vs. Phonology
     - Phonetics: Focuses on the physical properties of speech sounds.
     - Phonology: Examines the sound system and patterns of languages.
  Types of Phonetic Studies
  - Articulatory phonetics: Studies how sounds are produced by the mouth
     and vocal cords.
  - Acoustic phonetics: Analyzes the physical properties of speech sounds,
     like frequency and amplitude.
  - Auditory phonetics: Examines how listeners perceive speech sounds.
  - Experimental phonetics and phonology: Employs scientific methods to
     investigate phonetic and phonological phenomena.
  - Generative phonology: A theoretical framework that posits rules and
     constraints governing sound patterns in languages.
  Articulatory Phonetics-Speech Production
Articulatory phonetics investigates how speech sounds are produced by the
articulators (lips, tongue, teeth, etc.).
     - Place of articulation: Where the sound is made (e.g., bilabial /p/).
     - Manner of articulation: How the sound is made (e.g., stop /p/).
     - Voicing: Whether the sound is voiced (e.g., /z/) or voiceless (e.g., /s/).

Sound Waves: Sound waves are the physical basis of speech. They are
created by the vibration of the vocal cords and travel through the air as
pressure waves.
The Oro-Nasal Process: The oro-nasal process refers to the coordination of
the oral and nasal cavities in speech production. Sounds can be made with
either an oral (mouth) or nasal (nose) articulation, or a combination of both.
Articulatory Gestures: Articulatory gestures are the movements and
positions of the articulators (lips, tongue, teeth, etc.) that produce speech
sounds.
Manners of Articulation: Manners of articulation refer to the way in which
the articulators interact to produce sounds.
Stop: Oral and Nasal
    - Oral stops: /p/, /t/, /k/ (made by blocking the airflow with the lips or
       tongue)
    - Nasal stops: /m/, /n/, /ŋ/ (made by allowing airflow through the nose)
Fricative: Fricatives are made by directing airflow through a narrow channel,
causing friction: /s/, /z/, /f/, /v/
Approximants: Approximants are made by directing airflow through a
relatively wide channel, with little friction: /w/, /j/, /r/
Trill, Tap and Flap
    - Trill: /r/ (made by rapid vibration of the tongue)
    - Tap: /ɾ/ (made by a quick touch of the tongue)
    - Flap: /ɾ/ (made by a quick movement of the tongue)
The Waveforms of Consonants: Consonant waveforms show the acoustic
characteristics of consonant sounds.
The Articulation of Vowel Sounds: Vowels are made by the free flow of air
through the vocal cords, with no obstruction by the articulators.
The Sounds of Vowels: Vowels have different qualities (e.g., /i/, /e/, /a/) and
can be long or short.
Long Vowels and Diphthongs
    - Long vowels: prolonged vowel sounds (e.g., /iː/, /eː/)
    - Diphthongs: gliding vowel sounds (e.g., /ai/, /au/)
Introduction to Suprasegmentals: Suprasegmentals refer to the prosodic
features of speech, such as intonation, stress, and rhythm.

Why Transcribe? Transcription helps to represent speech sounds in a
standardized way, facilitating communication and analysis.
Introduction to IPA: The International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) is a
standardized system for transcribing speech sounds. The IPA chart displays
the range of speech sounds, organized by place and manner of articulation.
Transcription of Vowels: Vowels are transcribed using symbols that
represent their quality and duration.
Transcription of Consonants: Consonants are transcribed using symbols
that represent their place, manner, and voicing.
Broad and Narrow Transcription
   - Broad transcription: represents speech sounds in a general way,
       without detailed phonetic information
   - Narrow transcription: represents speech sounds in a detailed and
       precise way, including phonetic features

Lesson-01
             INTRODUCTION TO THE COURSE-I
Topic 001: Introduction to the Course
What does this section cover?
It covers the overall sketch of the course, including aims, objectives, and
evaluation criteria.
What is the primary focus of this section?
The primary focus of this section is to provide an overview of the course,
including its aims, objectives, and the criteria used for evaluation.
Topic 002: Importance of Studying Phonetics and Phonology
What is linguistics?
Linguistics is the study of language structure and function.
How does phonetics and phonology fit into linguistics?
Phonetics and phonology study speech sounds and their patterns within language.
Why are phonetics and phonology important in linguistics?
They help understand how speech sounds are produced and change, aiding
language description and documentation.
Define linguistics and its scope.
Linguistics is the study of language and its components, encompassing how
language is structured and functions. It delves into various aspects like sounds,
words, sentences, meanings, and their interrelationships.

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                          1

How do phonetics and phonology contribute to linguistics?
Phonetics and phonology are integral to linguistics as they explore the sounds used
in human speech and their patterns within languages. This understanding aids in
language description, preservation, and analysis.
Elaborate on the significance of phonetics and phonology.
Phonetics and phonology play a pivotal role in deciphering speech sounds'
production, transformations, and variations, contributing to language
documentation, cross-linguistic comparisons, and typological studies.
Topic 003: Focus Language - English
Which language is the main focus of this course?
English is the main focus, specifically Received Pronunciation (RP) or British
English.
Are examples from other languages used in the course?
Yes, examples from local languages like Urdu, Punjabi, etc., are used for
comparisons.
Which language serves as the main focus of this course?
The main focus of this course is the English language, particularly the Received

COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                         1

Lip shape (rounded, neutral, or spread), tongue position (front, middle, or back),

How do vowels differ from consonants in terms of articulation, as explained?
it is elucidated that vowels and consonants differ in their articulation. Vowels are
characterized by the absence of complete closure in the mouth and the lack of
audible friction. Air flows evenly over the center of the tongue during vowel
articulation. Vowels are also typically found at the center of a syllable and are
rarely able to stand alone as a whole syllable. To distinguish one vowel from
another, phonetics considers properties such as lip shape (rounded, neutral, or
spread) and tongue position (front, middle, or back).
Topic-034: The Sounds of Vowels
How can vowels be defined phonetically?
Vowels are sounds without complete mouth closure or audible friction, with air
escaping over the center of the tongue.
What are the key acoustic features used to distinguish vowels?
Formant frequencies F1 and F2, with F1 related to vowel height and F2 related to
front or back vowel qualities.

What is the significance of long vowels in some languages?
Long vowels can create phonemic distinctions between short and long vowel
sounds, impacting stress patterns.

A diphthong contains a glide from one vowel quality to another. BBC English has
eight diphthongs.
What is the significance of long vowels in some languages, as discussed?

hold significance in certain languages. These long vowels create a contrast of

important in speech, with stressed syllables typically being longer than unstressed
ones. Some languages, like English, have phonemic differences between short and
long vowels, contrasting short vowels (e.g., i, e, ɒ, υ, ə) with long vowels (e.g., iː,

Pitch, loudness, tempo, juncture, syllable, rhythm, and stress.

What does 'suprasegmental' refer to in phonetics?
'Suprasegmental' refers to aspects of sound like intonation, which go beyond

 Topic-037: Why Transcribe?
What is transcription in phonetics and phonology?
Transcription is the writing down of a spoken utterance using specific symbols.
Why is transcription important in phonetics, and what is the difference
between phonemic and phonetic transcription?
Transcription is vital for representing spoken language. It can be divided into
phonemic, where only symbols for phonemes are used, and phonetic, which
provides more detailed information about sounds.
Topic-038: Introduction to IPA
What is the IPA (International Phonetic Association), and when was it
established?
The IPA, established in 1886, is a forum that uses phonetics to enhance foreign
language teaching.
How did the IPA influence language teaching, and how does it contribute to
phonetic study today?
The IPA revolutionized language teaching, shifting focus from written language to
spoken language proficiency. Today, it provides tools for phonetic study and
maintains a set of alphabets for transcription.

Describe nasals.

Like stops, nasal can also occur voiced or voiceless (for example, in Burmese, Ukrainian and French)
though in English and other most languages nasals are voiced. As voiceless nasals are comparatively
rare, they are symbolized simply by adding the voiceless diacritic [ ] under the symbol for the voiced
sound. There are no special symbols for voiceless nasals and it is written as /m/ - a combination of the
letter for the voiced bilabial nasal and a diacritic indicating voicelessness.

Q. Explain Fricatives

        Fricative as an articulatory gesture may be divided into voiced or voiceless sounds but we can
also subdivide fricatives in accordance with other aspects of the gestures that produce them. For
example, some authorities have divided fricatives into sounds such as [s], in which the tongue is
grooved so that the airstream comes out through a narrow channel, and those such as [θ], in which the
tongue is flat and forms a wide slit through which the air flows. On the other hand, a slightly better
way of dividing fricatives is to separate them into groups on a purely auditory basis.

Q. Define sibilant sounds.

The fricatives [s, z, ʒ, ʃ] are called sibilant sounds. They have more acoustic energy—that is, greater
loudness—at a higher pitch than the other fricative sounds.

Q. What are gestures?

In phonetics and phonology, speech sounds (segments) using basic units of contrast are defined as
gestures.

Q. What are Articulatory Targets?

All consonants have a fixed articulatory target which is realised at a single precise place
of articulation. The articulatory target for a particular consonant is known as its target for a particular
consonant is known as its articulatory locus.
The traditional terms which are used for all the places of articulation are not just names for particular
locations (on the roof of the mouth). They should be thought of as names for articulatory targets.

Q. Write down types of Articulatory Gestures.

i. Bilabial gesture – (e.g., stops and nasal: p, b, m). The symbols for the voiceless and voiced bilabial
fricatives are [ɸβ]. These sounds are pronounced by bringing the two lips nearly together, so that there
is only a slit between them.

ii. Labiodental fricatives – [f, v]. In English, a labiodental nasal, [ɱ], may occur when /m/ occurs
before /f/, as in emphasis or symphony.

iii. Dental - e.g. dental fricatives [θ, ð] but there are no dental stops, nasals, or laterals except
allophonically realized (before [θ, ð] as in eighth, tenth, wealth). any speakers of rench, Italian,
and other languages (such as rdu, ashto and indhi typically have dental stops such as [t d].

iv. Alveolar are very common targets and stops, nasals, and fricatives all occur in English and in
many other languages at alveolar as a target of articulatory gestures (e.g., t, d, n, l, r., etc.).

v. Retroflex is very common sound in many Pakistani languages which is made by curling the tip of
the tongue up and back so that the tongue tip moves during the retroflex sounds such as [ɳ, ŋ, ɲ, ʈ, ɽ].

vii. Palato-alveolar and palatal are also possible articulatory gestures commonly found in world
languages. Similarly, velar sounds found in Urdu and other Pakistani languages need to be mentioned
here including [x, ɣ] which are velar fricatives. The gestures for pharyngeal (such as Arabic
pharyngeal fricative [ʕ] and epiglottal sounds (such as epiglottal fricative [ʢ] involve pulling the root
of the tongue or the epiglottis back toward the back wall of the pharynx.
